title: MoSSP: Momentum-Based Stochastic Penalty for Constrained Optimization
one_liner: A single-loop method using random mini-batches that solves constrained optimization problems where the cost has a special two-part structure by adding penalty terms and momentum to keep solutions on track.
lead: When you have a large learning problem with constraints that must be satisfied, existing methods either run in nested loops (slow) or ignore the special structure of the cost function. MoSSP solves this by wrapping the entire problem — constraints and all — into one efficient loop with momentum, without sacrificing mathematical guarantees.

problem.h2: The nested-loop trap in constrained learning
paras: When you train a model with constraints (for example, a classifier that must also stay fair across groups, or a regressor that must satisfy bounds), you face a hard choice. You can solve the constraint inside a loop (update the model, check the constraint, adjust, repeat) but this takes forever on large datasets. Or you can ignore the special structure of your cost function and use a generic method, which throws away information and becomes inefficient.

A beginner might try running the full constraint check and solution step inside each training iteration — nested loops. This is mathematically sound but glacially slow. The real problem: nobody has figured out how to finish all the constraint work in just one pass per step, with mathematical guarantees that you will actually converge.

callout.html: Add penalty terms (soft constraints) to the cost, take steps using random mini-batch data toward lower cost by wrapping the problem with its penalty, and use momentum to keep from wandering off the feasible region.

steps.text: Add soft penalty terms that push toward feasibility as part of the cost.
Pick a random mini-batch from your data; the pattern in it points the direction toward lower cost, because the error on that small sample reflects the overall error direction.

Move toward lower cost using the direction shown by mini-batch data, then resolve any hard constraint via a projection, because one step moves you and the projection snaps you back to legal territory.
Update the step using past movement history to smooth out randomness, because averaging multiple noisy directions cancels noise and leaves the true direction.
One loop per iteration; no inner solve needed.

paras: The paper changes the constraint-handling mechanism itself. Instead of solving constraints in a nested inner loop, it folds them into the cost function via penalty terms and solves the augmented problem with a single step per iteration that uses a technique called proximal mapping to handle hard constraints alongside the cost reduction.

hidden.h2: The KKT gap — how close you are to the solution
hidden.name: KKT (Karush-Kuhn-Tucker) gap
paras: The KKT conditions are a set of equations that a true solution must satisfy. They check three things: the gradient is zero (or balanced by constraints), the constraints are satisfied, and the penalty terms are in the right direction. The KKT gap measures how far you are from meeting all three at once — it is not just whether your cost is low, but whether you have actually solved the constrained problem correctly.

The paper proves that MoSSP finds points where this gap shrinks to a target size epsilon in a finite number of gradient samples. This is the hidden quantity being controlled: not final accuracy (which is easy to fake by running longer), but the actual mathematical proof that you are near the solution.

heat.caption: Darker means bigger KKT gap (farther from solution); highlights mark where penalties are largest.

reads.html: The KKT gap tells you whether your model actually obeys the constraints and has stopped improving, not just whether your loss number is small.
The paper proves how many times you need to look at random mini-batches of data (count gradient evaluations) to reach a point that is epsilon-close to the KKT conditions.

mechanism.h2: Why penalties plus momentum solve the problem
paras: The core insight is that you can turn a constrained problem into an unconstrained one by adding penalty terms to the cost. When you violate a constraint, the penalty jumps up; when you satisfy it, the penalty vanishes. A single step based on random mini-batch data naturally pushes you toward both low objective and feasibility in one shot.

Momentum is the second ingredient. Because you are using random mini-batches, each step direction estimate is noisy. Without momentum, this randomness causes you to zig-zag and converge slowly. Momentum averages past steps, so noise cancels out and you march steadily toward the solution. The combination — penalties that unify the goal, plus momentum that smooths randomness — lets you solve constrained problems in one loop with the same efficiency as unconstrained methods.

stages.s: Estimate gradient of cost plus penalties
Move a step in negative gradient direction
Blend with momentum from previous step

math.h2: The optimization step with penalty and momentum
math.words: x_new = (1 minus beta) times x_current plus beta times result, where result is the penalty-wrapped cost with a proximal step
math.equation: x_t+1 = (1 - beta) * x_t + beta * prox_step( gradient_of(f_convex + penalty * g_concave) )
symbols: the easy part of the cost to minimize
the hard part (concave), applied as a penalty
weighting on how much we care about constraints

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Say current weights are x_t = 0, and the gradient of the wrapped cost is 2.0 (pointing toward lower cost).
Take a step: gradient_step = 0 - 0.1 * 2.0 = -0.2 (we moved in the negative direction by 0.1 times the gradient).
Because beta is high, momentum is strong: we move 0.18 in the direction suggested, not a full 0.2. This is the averaging effect.

math.note: The penalty term ensures that each step implicitly makes progress toward feasibility, while momentum prevents random noise in the gradient from throwing you off track.

bars.h2: How convergence improves with the method

charts.title: Nested-loop approach
charts.note: Inner loop repeats constraint-checking; high overhead per iteration.

charts.title: MoSSP single-loop
charts.note: Fold penalties into cost; momentum stabilizes; one pass per step.

items.html: If the penalty term dominates the cost, the optimizer spends all effort on feasibility and ignores the main objective. The solution is feasible but far from optimal.
If the penalty is weak, constraints are violated with impunity and the algorithm drifts into infeasible regions. You must tune this by hand.
The theory assumes the hard part of the cost can be handled by a proximal mapping; if it is pathological, the algorithm may stall.

items.b: Done right: adaptive penalty and strong momentum.
items.html: Start with a modest penalty and increase it as the algorithm runs, or choose it based on problem structure. Use momentum strong enough to smooth randomness (beta close to 0.9) but not so high it lags behind sharp turns. With both calibrated, the method converges reliably.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Set up a constrained least-squares problem: minimize squared error subject to the solution staying within a ball (an upper bound on weight magnitude). Implement MoSSP with two variants — vanilla Polyak momentum and recursive momentum — and compare to a standard nested-loop solver on the same problem over 1000 iterations. Measure the KKT gap (how close to satisfying the conditions) and the total computation time. MoSSP should converge faster because it avoids nested loops, and the recursive variant should beat Polyak momentum because it refines the momentum calculation to track the problem more precisely.
demo.closing: MoSSP should reach the same KKT gap in half the iterations and solve the problem in one-third the wall-clock time.
